title: Translation, Reflection, Rotation and Enlargement
kicker: Cambridge Lower Secondary · Mathematics 0862 · Stage 8 · Geometry and Measure
summary: Translate with column vectors, reflect in lines such as x = 2, y = x and y = −x, rotate with a centre, angle and direction, and enlarge from a centre with a scale factor — and describe each transformation fully, with worked examples and a practice quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: **Translate** points and 2D shapes using a **column vector**, and know that the image is **congruent** to the object (same shape and same size) (8Gp.03)

**Reflect** points and shapes in a mirror line on or parallel to the x- or y-axis (x = a, y = b), or in **y = x** or **y = −x**; **identify** a reflection and write the equation of its mirror line (8Gp.04)
Know that a rotation needs a **centre**, a **direction** and an **angle**, and use these to perform and to describe rotations (8Gp.05)
**Enlarge** shapes from a **centre of enlargement** (outside or on the shape) with a positive whole-number **scale factor**; **identify** an enlargement, its centre and its scale factor (8Gp.06)

blocks.text: A **transformation** moves or changes a shape. The starting shape is the **object**; the new shape is the **image**. If the object is A, we often call the image A′ (say “A dash”). At Stage 8 you must be able to do four transformations on a coordinate grid **and** describe each one **fully** — that means giving every piece of information somebody else would need to repeat it exactly.

blocks.text: 1. Translation with column vectors

In a **translation** every point of the shape moves the **same distance in the same direction**. The shape does not turn or flip, so the image is **congruent** to the object and points the same way. At Stage 8 we describe a translation with a **column vector**: two numbers written one above the other in tall brackets.

blocks.caption: The column vector with top number 3 and bottom number −2 means 3 squares right and 2 squares down.

blocks.text: On this web page we type a column vector on one line as **(3 over −2)** — top number 3, bottom number −2. In your test paper, always write it as a column, top number above bottom number, inside tall brackets. **Never** write a vector like a coordinate (3, −2): coordinates are a position, a vector is a movement.

items: Read the vector: top number = move across (positive → right, negative → left); bottom number = move up or down (positive → up, negative → down).
Using coordinates: **add** the top number to every x-coordinate and **add** the bottom number to every y-coordinate.
Plot the new vertices and join them in the same order. Label the image (e.g. A′).
Check: the image must be the same size and the same way round as the object.

blocks.text: **Finding the vector of a translation.** Choose one vertex of the object and the matching vertex of the image. Vector = (image x − object x) over (image y − object y). Always work **from the object to the image**. Going back from A′ to A uses the opposite vector **(−6 over 4)**.
2. Reflection in a mirror line

In a **reflection**, each point of the image is the **same perpendicular distance** from the mirror line as the matching point of the object, but on the other side. Points on the mirror line do not move. The image is congruent to the object but **flipped** (its vertices go round the other way).

**Equations of mirror lines.** Every point on a vertical line has the same x-coordinate, so the line is **x = a number**. Every point on a horizontal line has the same y-coordinate, so the line is **y = a number**. The **x-axis** is the line y = 0 and the **y-axis** is the line x = 0. The two diagonal lines through the origin are **y = x** (points like (2, 2), (−3, −3)) and **y = −x** (points like (2, −2), (−3, 3)).

You do not need to learn the last two rows as formulas: just count. For the line x = 1, the point (3, 1) is 2 squares to the right of the line, so its image is 2 squares to the left of the line, at x = −1.

blocks.text: **Reflecting in a diagonal line on a grid.** Move from each vertex to the mirror line **diagonally across the squares** (at right angles to the line), then the same number of diagonal steps on the other side. For y = x you can also just swap the coordinates: (2, −1) → (−1, 2), (4, −1) → (−1, 4), (4, 1) → (1, 4).

**Identifying a reflection.** If a shape and its image are congruent but the image is flipped, it is a reflection. To find the mirror line, take a vertex and its image: the mirror line goes through the **midpoint** of the two points and is at right angles to the line joining them. Example: (2, 5) and its image (2, −1). The midpoint is (2, 2), and the points are one above the other, so the mirror line is horizontal: **y = 2**.
3. Rotation: centre, angle and direction

In a **rotation**, the shape **turns** around a fixed point, the **centre of rotation**. You need **three** facts to rotate a shape or to describe a rotation — if one is missing, the rotation is not fully described:

items: the **centre** of rotation, as coordinates, e.g. (−1, 0) — it can be inside, on or outside the shape;
the **angle**: usually 90° (a quarter turn), 180° (a half turn) or 270° (three quarters of a turn);
the **direction**: **clockwise** (the way clock hands turn) or **anticlockwise**. A 180° turn is the same in both directions, so the direction is not needed for 180°.

blocks.text: **Method 1 — tracing paper (allowed in the test).** Trace the object and mark the centre on the tracing. Put your pencil point on the centre, turn the tracing through the angle in the given direction (a quarter turn for 90°), then press through or copy the vertices on to the grid underneath.

**Method 2 — the “arm” method.** From the centre, describe each vertex as a move across and a move up or down. Turn that move through the angle: in a 90° **clockwise** turn, **up becomes right, right becomes down, down becomes left and left becomes up**. Then step out from the centre with the new move.

blocks.text: **Identifying a rotation.** If the image is congruent, **not** flipped, but pointing a different way, it is a rotation. Look at how one side has turned to find the angle and direction (a horizontal side that becomes vertical has turned 90°). Find the centre by trying points with tracing paper: the correct centre is the point that, when you hold it still and turn the tracing, takes the object exactly on to the image. The centre is the same distance from a vertex and from that vertex’s image.
4. Enlargement: centre and scale factor

An **enlargement** changes the size of a shape. Every length is multiplied by the **scale factor**, and all angles stay the same, so the image is **similar** to the object (same shape, different size) — not congruent. At Stage 8 the scale factor is a positive whole number (2, 3, 4…). The **centre of enlargement** is the fixed point that all distances are measured from; it can be outside the shape or on it.

items: For one vertex, count how far it is from the centre: across and up/down (e.g. 2 right, 1 up).
Multiply **both** distances by the scale factor (scale factor 2: 4 right, 2 up).
Count that far **from the centre** (not from the vertex!) and mark the image vertex.
Repeat for every vertex, join them up, and check: each side of the image should be (scale factor) × the matching side of the object.
Extra check: the centre, a vertex and its image are always on one straight line (a ray).

blocks.text: **Centre on the shape.** If the centre is a vertex of the shape, that vertex stays where it is and the shape grows away from it. For example, enlarging the square with vertices (1, 1), (2, 1), (2, 2), (1, 2) by scale factor 3 with centre (1, 1) gives the square (1, 1), (4, 1), (4, 4), (1, 4).

**Identifying an enlargement.** (1) **Scale factor** = length of a side on the image ÷ length of the matching side on the object. (2) **Centre**: draw straight lines through each image vertex and its matching object vertex, and extend them. They all meet at one point: the centre of enlargement.

blocks.title: بالعربي: اوصف التحويل كاملًا
items: الانتقال (translation): اكتب المتجه العمودي — الرقم اللي فوق = يمين (+) أو شمال (−)، والرقم اللي تحت = فوق (+) أو تحت (−).
الانعكاس (reflection): اكتب معادلة خط المرآة، مثلًا x = 2 أو y = −1 أو y = x.
الدوران (rotation): لازم 3 حاجات: المركز + الزاوية + الاتجاه (مع أو عكس عقارب الساعة).
التكبير (enlargement): لازم حاجتين: المركز + معامل التكبير. وقيس المسافات دايمًا من المركز.
الثلاثة الأولى صورتهم متطابقة (congruent) مع الأصل، أما التكبير فالصورة متشابهة (similar) بس.

blocks.text: Worked examples

**Worked example 1** — Translation  [2 marks]
Triangle P has vertices (−4, 1), (−2, 1) and (−4, 4). It is translated by the vector **(5 over −3)**. Write the coordinates of the vertices of the image.

items: Top number 5: add 5 to every x-coordinate. Bottom number −3: subtract 3 from every y-coordinate.

blocks.text:
**Answer:** (1, −2), (3, −2) and (1, 1). Mark scheme style: 2 marks for all three correct; 1 mark for two correct.
**Common mistake:** moving 3 **up** because the 3 looks positive. The bottom number is −3, so the move is down.

**Worked example 2** — Describing a translation  [2 marks]
Shape A is translated to shape B. The vertex (1, 2) of A moves to the vertex (−3, 5) of B. Describe fully the single transformation that maps A on to B.

items: Across: −3 − 1 = −4 (4 left).
Up/down: 5 − 2 = 3 (3 up).
A full description names the transformation **and** gives the vector.

blocks.text:
**Answer:** a **translation** by the vector **(−4 over 3)** (1 mark for “translation”, 1 mark for the vector).
**Common mistake:** writing “move 4 left and 3 up” without the word translation, or writing the vector as a coordinate (−4, 3).

**Worked example 3** — Reflection in y = x and y = −x  [2 marks]
The point M is (5, −2). Write the coordinates of the image of M after (a) a reflection in the line y = x, (b) a reflection in the line y = −x.

items: (a) Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates: (5, −2) → (−2, 5).
(b) Reflection in y = −x swaps the coordinates **and** changes both signs: (5, −2) → (2, −5).
Check (b): is M above or below the line y = −x? At x = 5 the line is at y = −5, and M is at y = −2, so M is above the line; its image (2, −5) is below it (at x = 2 the line is at y = −2). ✓

blocks.text:
**Answer:** (a) (−2, 5)  (b) (2, −5)
**Common mistake:** in (b), swapping the numbers but forgetting to change the signs, giving (−2, 5) again.

**Worked example 4** — Identifying a mirror line  [1 mark]
The point (−1, 3) is reflected to the point (5, 3). Write the equation of the mirror line.

items: The y-coordinates are the same, so the points are side by side and the mirror line is **vertical**: x = something.
The mirror line is halfway between them: x = (−1 + 5) ÷ 2 = 2.

blocks.text:
**Answer:** x = 2
**Common mistake:** writing y = 2. A vertical line has an equation x = …, because every point on it has the same x-coordinate.

**Worked example 5** — Rotation  [2 marks]
Triangle R has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1) and (1, 2). Rotate R 90° clockwise about the centre (−1, 0). Write the coordinates of the image. (See the diagram in section 3.)

**Answer:** (0, −2), (0, −4) and (1, −2). Check: the side from (1, 1) to (3, 1) was horizontal, length 2; the image side from (0, −2) to (0, −4) is vertical, length 2 ✓.
**Common mistake:** rotating about the origin or about a vertex of the shape instead of the centre you were given.

**Worked example 6** — Enlargement  [2 marks]
Triangle E has vertices (2, 2), (4, 2) and (2, 3). Enlarge E by scale factor 2 with centre (0, 1). (See the diagram in section 4.)

**Answer:** (4, 3), (8, 3) and (4, 5). Check: base 2 → 4 and height 1 → 2, both doubled ✓.
**Common mistake:** making the shape twice as big but drawing it in the wrong place (for example, adding 2 to the coordinates). The position depends on the centre.

**Worked example 7** — Identifying an enlargement  [3 marks]
In the diagram in section 4, shape A has vertices (2, 2), (3, 2), (3, 4) and shape B has vertices (4, 4), (7, 4), (7, 10). Describe fully the single transformation that maps A on to B.

items: B is bigger and the same shape, so it is an **enlargement**.
Scale factor: base of A = 3 − 2 = 1; base of B = 7 − 4 = 3. 3 ÷ 1 = **3**. (Check the heights: 2 and 6 ✓.)
Centre: draw lines through (4, 4) and (2, 2), and through (7, 4) and (3, 2), and through (7, 10) and (3, 4). They meet at **(1, 1)**.
Check with the vector method: (2, 2) is 1 right and 1 up from (1, 1); × 3 gives 3 right and 3 up → (4, 4) ✓.

blocks.text:
**Answer:** an **enlargement**, scale factor **3**, centre **(1, 1)** — 1 mark for each part.
**Common mistake:** giving only “enlargement scale factor 3”. Without the centre the description is not full and loses a mark.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up the two numbers of a column vector. Top = across (x), bottom = up/down (y).
Writing a vector like a coordinate pair. A vector goes in a tall bracket with one number above the other.
Writing a vertical mirror line as y = … . Vertical lines are x = …; horizontal lines are y = … .
Reflecting in y = −x by swapping only. You must swap the coordinates **and** change both signs.
Measuring the distance to a diagonal mirror line straight across the grid instead of at right angles to the line.
Describing a rotation without the centre, the angle **or** the direction (all three are needed, except that 180° needs no direction).
Enlarging by counting from the shape instead of from the centre of enlargement.
Giving the scale factor as “+3” or “3 times bigger in area”. The scale factor is about **lengths**: every length × 3.
Using two transformations when the question asks for **a single transformation**.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: “Translate the shape by the vector …” or “Draw the image of shape A after …” on a printed grid — vertices must be exactly on grid points; use a ruler.

“Describe fully the single transformation that maps shape A on to shape B” — usually 2 or 3 marks: 1 for the name and 1 for each piece of information (vector; mirror line; centre, angle and direction; centre and scale factor).
“Write the equation of the mirror line” — answer like x = 3 or y = −x.
“Write the coordinates of the image of point P” — quick coordinate rules save time; check with a sketch.
Tick or ring questions such as “Which transformation gives an image that is not congruent?”.
Tracing paper is allowed in the test: use it for rotations and to check reflections.
When you identify an enlargement, draw the rays in pencil on the diagram — markers can then see your method.

blocks.title: خلي بالك
items: خط رأسي = x = رقم، وخط أفقي = y = رقم. محور x نفسه هو y = 0.
الانعكاس في y = x: بدّل الرقمين. في y = −x: بدّل الرقمين وغيّر الإشارتين.
في التكبير عُد المسافات من مركز التكبير مش من الشكل، واضربها في معامل التكبير.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Transformations — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. A column vector is typed here as (top over bottom). Use squared paper and tracing paper. For the drawing and explaining questions, mark yourself with the mark scheme shown after you finish.

questions.q: Which transformation can give an image that is **not** congruent to the object?
questions.e: Translations, reflections and rotations keep the same shape and size, so the image is congruent. An enlargement with scale factor 3 makes every length 3 times longer, so the image is similar, not congruent.

questions.q: The point (3, −2) is translated by the vector (−5 over 4) — top number −5, bottom number 4. Write the coordinates of the image.
questions.e: Add the top number to x: 3 + (−5) = −2. Add the bottom number to y: −2 + 4 = 2. Image: (−2, 2).

questions.q: Which mirror line maps every point (a, b) to the point (b, a)?
questions.e: Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates, e.g. (4, 1) → (1, 4). The x-axis gives (a, −b), the y-axis gives (−a, b) and y = −x gives (−b, −a).

questions.q: The point (3, 5) is reflected in the line y = −x. Write the coordinates of its image.
questions.e: In y = −x, swap the coordinates and change both signs: (3, 5) → (−5, −3). Check: the midpoint of (3, 5) and (−5, −3) is (−1, 1), which is on y = −x ✓.

questions.q: The point (−2, 3) is reflected in the line x = 1. Write the coordinates of its image.
questions.e: x = 1 is a vertical line. (−2, 3) is 3 squares to the left of it, so the image is 3 squares to the right: x = 1 + 3 = 4. The y-coordinate does not change. Image: (4, 3).

questions.e: Matching vertices: (1, 1) and (1, −3). They are one above the other, so the mirror line is horizontal. Halfway between y = 1 and y = −3 is y = (1 + (−3)) ÷ 2 = −1. The mirror line is y = −1.

questions.q: Which rotation always gives the same image as a rotation of 90° clockwise about the same centre?
questions.e: A full turn is 360°. Turning 90° one way ends in the same place as turning 360° − 90° = 270° the other way. So 90° clockwise = 270° anticlockwise.

questions.q: The point (3, 1) is rotated 90° clockwise about the origin (0, 0). Write the coordinates of its image.
questions.e: (3, 1) is 3 right and 1 up from the origin. A clockwise quarter turn makes right → down and up → right: 3 down and 1 right, i.e. (1, −3). Rule: (a, b) → (b, −a).

questions.q: (c) Write the coordinates of the centre of enlargement.
questions.e: Join (6, 5) to (4, 3), (8, 5) to (5, 3) and (8, 7) to (5, 4), and extend the lines: they meet at (2, 1). Check: (4, 3) is 2 right, 2 up from (2, 1); × 2 gives 4 right, 4 up → (6, 5) ✓.

questions.q: Ali says: “A rotation of 180° about (0, 0) maps (4, 2) to (−4, 2).” Is Ali correct? Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: Not correct, with a correct reason, e.g. a 180° rotation about the origin changes the signs of both coordinates, so the image is (−4, −2); OR (−4, 2) is the reflection in the y-axis. Accept a correct sketch with explanation.
questions.e: A half turn about the origin sends (a, b) to (−a, −b), so (4, 2) → (−4, −2). Ali changed only the x-coordinate — that is a reflection in the y-axis, not a rotation.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Translation: column vector (top = across, bottom = up/down). Add the vector to every vertex. The image is congruent.

Reflection: same perpendicular distance on the other side of the mirror line. Vertical lines are x = …, horizontal lines are y = …; y = x swaps the coordinates, y = −x swaps them and changes both signs.
Rotation: always give the centre, the angle and the direction (no direction needed for 180°). 90° clockwise = 270° anticlockwise.
Enlargement: multiply the distances **from the centre** by the scale factor. Scale factor = image length ÷ object length; find the centre where the rays through matching vertices meet.
“Describe fully” = name of the transformation + all its details. Only enlargement changes the size.
